history.heading: Saint Helena
paragraphs: Saint Helena, a remote volcanic island in the South Atlantic, was discovered uninhabited by the Portuguese in 1502. The English East India Company took control in 1659 and used it as a supply stop for ships sailing between Europe and Asia.

After his defeat at Waterloo, Napoleon Bonaparte was exiled to Saint Helena, where he died in 1821; his house at Longwood is French property. The island was also a base against the slave trade, where thousands of liberated Africans were landed in the 19th century. The opening of the Suez Canal in 1869 reduced its importance.

history.heading: Ascension and Tristan da Cunha
paragraphs: Ascension Island, garrisoned by Britain from 1815 to guard against Napoleon's rescue, later became a communications and military base used by the UK and US. Tristan da Cunha, settled in 1816, is the most remote inhabited archipelago in the world; its population was evacuated after a volcanic eruption in 1961 and returned in 1963.

culture.heading: Saints and islanders
paragraphs: Residents of Saint Helena, known as "Saints", have mixed European, African and Asian ancestry and speak English. Jonathan, a giant tortoise living on the island, is thought to be the oldest living land animal, hatched around 1832. Tristan da Cunha has about 250 residents sharing just a handful of surnames.

politics.heading: British Overseas Territory
paragraphs: Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha form a single British Overseas Territory with a governor based on Saint Helena. Each island has its own council. Ascension has no permanent population with right of abode.

economy.heading: Small economies
paragraphs: Saint Helena's economy relies on British aid, public services and small-scale tourism; an airport opened in 2017. It produces coffee and fish. Tristan da Cunha earns income from rock lobster fishing and stamps, and Ascension's economy centres on its military base. The Saint Helena pound is at par with the British pound.
